title: Threat Intelligence Sharing
summary: Threat intelligence sharing is the controlled exchange of information about adversaries, campaigns and indicators between organisations, sector groups and trusted communities. It works through structured representation and transport mechanisms such as Structured Threat Information Expression for describing objects and relationships, and Trusted Automated Exchange of Intelligence Information for moving them, with trust groups and handling markings deciding who may see what and how far it may be redistributed. In real environments it appears as sector information sharing and analysis centres, vendor intelligence feeds, and machine to machine feeds that populate detection platforms and blocklists. The mistake organisations make is measuring success by volume: unvetted indicators produce false positives, age quickly, and can leak detail that identifies the victim. Effective programmes share behaviour and detection logic rather than only addresses, apply handling rules, and verify what they receive before it drives automated blocking.

beginner.definition: Threat intelligence sharing means organisations telling each other what attacks they have seen. Threat intelligence is information about attackers, their tools and their targets. Sharing lets one company warn the others before the same attack arrives. Groups agree on rules about what may be shared and with whom.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attackers often reuse the same tools against many similar organisations. If one victim warns the others quickly, the next attack may be stopped early. Small teams gain knowledge they could never gather alone. Sharing also helps a whole industry see a campaign that no single member could spot. Without clear rules, sharing can expose a victim or spread false alarms to everyone.
howItWorks: An organisation detects an attack on its own network and carefully records what the intruder did.
Analysts remove details that could identify their own company or its customers.
They convert the findings into a common format that other security tools can read.
They send the report to a trusted group under agreed handling rules.
Receiving teams check the shared information against their own systems, logs and network records.
They confirm or reject the indicators and send feedback to improve the feed.
beginner.example: Think of a neighbourhood watch group in a row of shops. One shopkeeper sees a thief try a particular trick at closing time. She tells the group, describing the trick and not the private details of her shop. The other shopkeepers then check their own doors for the same trick. Nobody shares customer lists. Threat intelligence sharing follows that habit: useful warnings, shared inside agreed limits.
takeaways: Sharing lets one victim protect many others from the same campaign.
Remove anything that identifies your organisation or your customers before you share.
Verify what you receive before using it to block traffic automatically.

objectives: Explain what threat intelligence sharing is and who takes part.
Describe the role of common formats for representing and transporting intelligence.
Explain why handling rules and trust groups are necessary.
Describe how a receiving team validates shared indicators before acting.
Explain the risks of sharing without removing victim detail.
Identify why behaviour based reporting ages better than address lists.
